flashcards.q: What makes a code change actually a 'refactor' versus a rewrite mislabeled as one?
flashcards.a: Behavior preservation, verified by running tests before and after each small step. If observable behavior changes, it's a feature change or rewrite and deserves that level of review scrutiny, not the lighter trust a true refactor earns.

flashcards.q: What smell does Replace Conditional with Polymorphism respond to, and what's the concrete payoff?
flashcards.a: A switch/if-chain branching on an object's type, repeated across multiple call sites. Payoff: adding a new type becomes adding one new subclass instead of finding and editing every scattered switch statement.

flashcards.q: What is Feature Envy, and which refactor targets it?
flashcards.a: A method that uses another class's data and methods more than its own class's -- a sign it's living on the wrong class. Move Method relocates it to the class whose data it actually operates on.

flashcards.q: What is the Strangler Fig pattern and what architectural component makes it work?
flashcards.a: A legacy-migration strategy where a routing layer (proxy/flag/gateway) sits in front of the legacy system, migrating one capability at a time with per-capability cutover. The legacy system stays fully operational the entire time -- the router is the component that makes gradual, reversible cutover possible.

flashcards.q: What early-velocity numbers predict strangler migration success or failure (41 enterprise migrations, 2022-2025)?
flashcards.a: 68% of migrations stall before 90 days without replacing their first monolith component. Projects extracting under 5% of monolith functionality in the first 90 days had a 92% failure rate.

flashcards.q: Why is the 90-day velocity number an organizational predictor rather than a technical one?
flashcards.a: The first quarter is disproportionately spent on invisible infrastructure (router, shadow-comparison tooling) producing no visible business value. If that phase drags past 90 days, executive attention and budget commitment erode before the architecture is tested at scale.

flashcards.q: Why is a big-bang legacy rewrite structurally riskier than a strangler migration?
flashcards.a: Requirements are frozen while the business's real needs keep evolving during the long build, and the cutover is all-or-nothing with no partial-success path -- if something's wrong, it's wrong for the whole system at once, at the worst possible moment.

flashcards.q: What is a shadow-traffic (dark-launch) phase in a strangler migration, and why skip it is dangerous?
flashcards.a: Running both legacy and new implementations in parallel against real traffic, diffing outputs, before cutting the router over for a capability. Skipping it means the first divergence is discovered in production after cutover, potentially as a customer-facing incident.

flashcards.q: Why can a strangler migration succeed technically but leave the legacy system running in production 18 months later?
flashcards.a: Cutting the router over per capability isn't the same as finishing the migration -- decommissioning the legacy code is a distinct milestone that's commonly skipped once organizational attention moves on after the highest-visibility capabilities migrate, leaving both systems running (doubled maintenance burden).

flashcards.q: What's the effective way to pitch refactoring time against a feature-hungry roadmap?
flashcards.a: Tie a specific, catalogue-named refactor to a specific, already-costed production event (incident hours, deploy risk, on-call cost) using the same currency the stakeholder already prioritizes features in -- not an abstract code-quality appeal.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't dependency-mapping tooling fully solve the 'six-month estimate becomes eighteen months' strangler failure mode?
flashcards.a: It reduces but doesn't eliminate the risk -- legacy codebases often have runtime-only coupling (shared database tables, timing assumptions, config-driven branching) that static call-graph analysis doesn't fully capture, so real testing still surfaces genuine surprises.
